newsitem.title: CHINA: China activists urge release of protest workers.
newsitem.headline: China activists urge release of protest workers.

text.p: Two Chinese dissidents have appealed to President Jiang Zemin to release workers detained for taking part this month in demonstrations against job losses, a human rights group said on Sunday.

Activists Shen Liangqing and Zhang Lin sent an open letter on Friday to Jiang, Premier Li Peng and National People's Congress Chairman Qiao Shi protesting against the treatment of workers involved in the protests in southwestern Sichuan province, the New York-based group Human Rights in China said.

"We hope for the realisation of complete modernisation of politics, the economy and society... through democratic and legal means," they wrote in their letter, a copy of which was faxed to news agencies.
Several thousand people staged demonstrations in Mianyang city in Sichuan on July 7 after at least three local state-run enterprises in the textile sector declared bankruptcy.
Police dispersed the angry factory workers and detained several leaders, local officials said. They dismissed reports that some were injured when the demonstrations were broken up.
Shen and Zhang, both from Hefei in eastern Anhui province, demanded the release of those detained, medical treatment for the wounded and an official investigation.
"We propose the Mianyang government make a formal apology to the masses for this incident, immediately release those detained and give medical treatment to the wounded," they wrote.

Shen, a former Anhui prosecutor, offered to take part in an investigation himself as an observer or prosecutor. Shen was jailed for 17 months for his role in the 1989 pro-democracy demonstrations that were crushed by the army with heavy loss of life.
The two dissidents called on the government to establish an effective social security system to protect workers' rights.
They accused Mianyang government leaders of covering up the mistakes of corrupt officials and disregarding workers' rights, party discipline and the law.

Shen last week sent an open letter to top leaders, warning that any attempt by Communist Party chief and state president Jiang to revive the title held by former Chairman Mao Zedong would start a slide deep into dictatorship.
Fellow activist Zhang, jailed for two years after the 1989 protests, last month completed three years of "re-education through labour" for his pro-democracy activities.

The international ICFTU labour movement was sharply critical on Friday of China China for breaking up the worker protests, citing the need for freedom of association and collective bargaining in the communist nation.
Worker unrest is one of the greatest fears of China's Communist Party leadership.
Reports of increasing numbers of daring protests by disgruntled workers have surfaced in recent years as economic reform has resulted in lay-offs from lumbering state factories.

China's leaders this year have placed reform of loss-making state enterprises at the top of their economic agenda, pushing through with bankruptcies that they had delayed for years for fear of social unrest.
